content.text: Picked my probes. Now I'll train two tasks that share no rules, then test one task that only recombines trained rules and one that uses only new rules.
Phase 1 showed no recombination benefit, so part-based looks unlikely. Next I'll train tasks that bring the probe's rules up to 2 occurrences each, then retest the probe.
Still no drop at 2 occurrences. Now I'll bring the probe's rules to 3 occurrences each, using tasks that are dissimilar to the probe.
After 3 occurrences the probe dropped sharply (several runs at 1 example). Now a control: retesting a task built from new rules to rule out a general improvement from extra training.

Probe P=L4-S1-M1 recombines only trained rules but has 0 similarity to the trained tasks. Its cost (mean about 29) matched a control made of new rules with low similarity, L3-S4-M2 (about 29), and was no better than a control made of new rules with higher similarity, L2-S3-M4 (about 24). So reusing rules gave no benefit, which argues against part-based. Phase 2: added L4-S1-M3 and L1-S2-M1, so L4, S1 and M1 each appeared twice, while P stayed at most 0.375 similar to any trained task. P was still about 32, which argues against k=2. Phase 3: added L4-S1-M4 and L1-S3-M1, so each rule appeared three times, and P stayed at most 0.375 similar. P dropped sharply (37,37,1,13,6,1,1,1, with 5 of 8 runs at or below 6), while the L3-S4-M2 control stayed the same (22,31,46,12). Recombination became cheap only once the rules had appeared 3 times, and this was not explained by similarity. This fits factor-when-justified with k=3, not holistic."}'

content.text:
I submitted **factor-when-justified** with 0.85 confidence. My best estimate is k = 3. I used 37 of the 60 budget.

The main probe was **L4-S1-M1**. It uses only rules the learner has been trained on, but its input-output mapping is very unlike every trained task (at most 0.375 similarity). Numbers below are examples to criterion.

| Stage | Training so far | Probe L4-S1-M1 | Control L3-S4-M2 (all new rules) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | L1-S1-M1, L4-S2-M3 (each probe rule seen once) | mean ≈ 29 (16, 39, 19, 38, 22, 38) | mean ≈ 29 (54, 25, 30, 12, 22) |
| 2 | + L4-S1-M3, L1-S2-M1 (each probe rule seen twice) | mean ≈ 32 (39, 48, 26, 14) | — |
| 3 | + L4-S1-M4, L1-S3-M1 (each probe rule seen 3 times) | 37, 37, 1, 13, 6, 1, 1, 1 | 22, 31, 46, 12 (unchanged) |

- **Against part-based:** at stage 1, a task built entirely from known rules was no cheaper than one built from new rules. A more similar all-new task (L2-S3-M4, mean ≈ 24) was if anything cheaper.
- **Against holistic:** the probe's similarity to the trained tasks was the same in stages 2 and 3, yet its cost collapsed only once each of its rules had appeared 3 times. The control stayed flat, so extra training in general doesn't explain the drop.
- **k = 3 rather than 2:** there was no improvement after 2 appearances.

**Caveats:**
- The noise is heavy: two of the eight stage-3 runs still came in at 37.
- I didn't test a second recombination task, so the drop rests on one probe.
- The evidence that k is 3 rather than 2 comes from only four samples at stage 2.
